What AI Cannot Do for You, According to the Man Who Automated His Entire Company

The most useful question about artificial intelligence is not what it can take over, but what you should refuse to hand it.

Stacey Chillemi

10 Min Read

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:39
Instaread

At seventeen, sleeping without a home and eating at a food bank in California, Gabe Campbell made a decision that had nothing to do with technology. He looked at what he described as a mountain too high to climb and realized he had two options. He could suffer for the rest of his life, or he could take full responsibility for everything that happened from that moment forward. “The best excuse in the world wasn’t really gonna change the circumstance,” he said. That choice, made years before he wrote a line of code, turns out to be the same choice millions of people are facing right now for entirely different reasons, as artificial intelligence rewrites what work is and what it is worth.

Gabe Campbell is the founder and CEO of AI Genesis LLC and the creator of aiOS, an AI product he designed and built. Before that, he worked as an AI architect and designer whose career included work with Google and BMW, where he helped build the electric vehicle app during the early scramble to figure out charging and grid load. He has published scientific studies on AI honesty and safe AGI frameworks. What makes his perspective unusual is not the resume. It is that he has lived at both ends of the range, from a bicycle and a food bank to the frontier of the technology everyone is currently anxious about, and he talks about both with the same plain language.

Why Taking Responsibility Is a Power Move, Not a Guilt Trip

The lesson Gabe Campbell drew from his worst year is easy to misread as tough love. It is actually a mechanism. When something goes wrong, he explained, you can point to the government, the recession, or the circumstance, and you may be objectively correct. The problem is what that conclusion costs you. “If you are okay with leaving it at that, what you’ve essentially said is that you have no ability to control it,” he said. “And that keeps you stuck.”

The reverse is also true, and this is the part worth holding onto. Accepting responsibility is frightening, but as Campbell put it, “when you accept that responsibility, which is scary, it also gives you the power to do something about it.” Responsibility and agency are the same object viewed from two sides. You cannot pick up one without the other. The practical version is simple: the next time you catch yourself building an airtight case for why a situation is not your fault, notice that the case, however true, hands your steering wheel to someone else.

The Price of a New Life Is Usually Your Old Safety

Gabe Campbell has quit twice from positions people told him he would be crazy to leave. He walked away from a sales job he was good at and hated, taught himself front-end development from YouTube videos and online courses, and spent about a year and a half in debt before it worked. Years later, with a comfortable app design career, he left again to go all in on AI. Both times, the people who loved him told him it was a mistake.

He does not describe those warnings as sabotage. They came from genuine care. But he offers a filter that clarifies whose input to weigh: “You never ask somebody for directions to a place they’ve never been.” The underlying pattern he names is more useful still. “Sometimes you have to sacrifice your old way of life and your old safety in order to enter a new bracket. That’s usually the cost.” Campbell is not arguing that everyone should quit something. He is pointing out that the discomfort you feel at the threshold is not evidence you chose wrong. It is often the toll.

The One Question He Uses to Turn a Setback Into a Next Step

After a promising deal with Mercedes-Benz collapsed because his one-person company was too small a risk for them, Gabe Campbell had to decide what the failure meant. What he landed on became the operating principle behind the way he now works in public about being the only human at his company.

He also carries a single question that he calls his secret weapon. When something goes badly, he asks: what would I have to do from this moment forward to turn this situation into a win? The question does two things at once. It skips the argument about fault, which changes nothing, and it forces the mind to produce a next action, which changes everything. Campbell is blunt about the alternative. Believing that a bad thing was unfair and disempowering may be accurate, but it does not improve the situation and it may prolong it.

Underneath all of it sits an observation he made about fear itself. What we are actually afraid of, he said, is rarely the circumstance. “We’re afraid of our emotions. We’re afraid of what we’ll feel if something happens.” He leans on Marcus Aurelius for the corrective: “You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this and you’ll find strength.” And on Seneca for the diagnosis, noting that the majority of human suffering happens in the imagination, since what has already happened is past and what has not happened has not happened.

What Artificial Intelligence Actually Does, One Step at a Time

Strip away the noise and the technology is less mysterious than it sounds. Every task a person does at work, Gabe Campbell explained, happens one step at a time. A machine can learn a step, and then it can repeat that step a thousand times without getting tired or bored. That is the whole of it. His framing for the moral panic is equally plain: “AI is just like money. It’s good in the hands of good people and it’s bad in the hands of bad people.”

Where he thinks people go wrong is in projecting human motives onto software. The fear that a powerful system will want to control us assumes a desire that Campbell argues machines simply do not have. “Control is a human emotion that comes from insecurity and fear,” he said. Machines have no impulse to start something, solve something, or dominate anything. That leaves humans, in his view, in the driver’s seat, holding the one thing that cannot be copied. As he put it, “I know how it feels to be human.”

The Test for What You Should Never Hand Over

That reframe is the most portable idea in the conversation, and it comes with a test anyone can run today. Campbell’s criteria are energy, purpose, and excitement. “What gives you energy? What gives you purpose? What excites you? That’s the stuff you keep.”

He applies it to himself without exception. He is a musician, and he will not automate the writing of a song or the idea behind it, because that work brings him joy. Tools that help the sound come out better once the idea exists are fair game. The distinction is not between important and unimportant work. It is between the work that returns something to you and the work that only drains. Campbell puts a fair question to the rest of it. Is it really human, he asked, to click a computer for eight hours a day doing something repetitive, and is that genuinely the thing we are afraid of losing?

Why Being Late to AI May Matter Less Than You Think

For anyone convinced they missed the window, Gabe Campbell offers a structural reason to relax. The field is moving so fast that formal training has lost much of its edge. “If you immerse yourself in it today, you’re gonna know just as much as anybody did yesterday,” he said. A month from now the tools will be different again, which means the gap between the expert and the beginner keeps resetting.

He is honest that something real is changing underneath. Since the Industrial Revolution, he noted, we have measured human worth by economic output, and that assumption is being tested now that execution and knowledge are being automated and commoditized. That is genuinely unsettling. It is also, in his view, the opening: a shot at doing work you actually love while the tasks you never loved get handled. His prescription borrows from Albert Einstein, who defined intelligence as the ability to adapt to change. Take one small step today to learn what this technology means for you specifically, rather than putting it off and staying stressed about it.

Campbell extends the same logic to safety at scale. He argues the safest way to roll out AI is equal access for everyone, drawing on the Cold War as his example, where mutual capability kept anyone from firing first. He has published studies and maintains a public repository on a framework he calls aiOS Presence, built around honesty and accountability. In his testing against leading models, he reports meaningful gains in honesty scores, and he has made the work public rather than proprietary for exactly that reason.

Fear Is the Only Thing That Reliably Costs You

The through line of Gabe Campbell’s story is not talent, and it is not timing. It is his refusal to let fear make the decision. “Don’t be afraid. Fear is disease,” he said, reaching for Franklin D. Roosevelt’s line about the only thing we have to fear being fear itself. He is not claiming fear disappears. He lived with it for years and simply concluded it never did much for him.

That connects to the standard he set for himself long before any of this worked. “I’d rather be excellent than right,” he said, meaning he would rather learn the hard truth about something he is doing badly than feel comfortable and stay wrong. It is also why he defines failure so narrowly. The only way to fail as a human being, in his view, is not to try, because a real hundred percent effort that does not work still leaves you with peace and permission to move on.

Here is the one thing to carry into your day. Take the task that drained you most this week and ask whether it gives you energy, purpose, or excitement. If the answer is no, it is a candidate to hand off. If the answer is yes, protect it, because that is the part of your work that is actually yours. Gabe Campbell built a company on that distinction, and he is the rare person qualified to say it from both sides of the machine.
